query:
We are building an automated alloy-discovery workflow that makes ~100 g batches of experimental
aluminium alloys by ULTRASONIC ATOMIZATION (AMAZEMET rePOWDER-class: induction heating, ceramic/graphite
crucible, argon atmosphere <50 ppm O2, melt dripped onto a vibrating sonotrode) to produce LPBF feedstock
powder. Alloys are Al-based with additions of Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn
at up to a few wt.% each.

We are considering a specific charging strategy and need the literature evidence for and against it:
INSTEAD of dosing aluminium powder, we would machine or form a small CUP / CRUCIBLE / CAPSULE OUT OF
HIGH-PURITY SOLID ALUMINIUM, robotically dispense only the NON-ALUMINIUM elemental and master-alloy
POWDERS into that aluminium cup, and then place the whole loaded aluminium cup inside the atomizer's
GRAPHITE (or ceramic) CRUCIBLE and melt it. The aluminium cup is sacrificial: it becomes the base metal
of the alloy. Please address, with citations and quantitative data wherever possible:

1. ALUMINIUM ENCAPSULATION OF ALLOY ADDITIONS. Is wrapping/encapsulating alloying elements, master alloys
   or elemental powders in aluminium (Al foil packets, Al cans, compacted Al-clad briquettes, "cored wire"
   with an aluminium sheath) an established practice for adding solutes to aluminium melts? What is the
   measured effect on RECOVERY / assimilation yield of the addition, on oxidation loss, and on dross
   formation, compared with adding loose powder to an open melt? Quantitative recovery percentages for
   elements such as Mg, Mn, Cr, Ti, Zr, Sc, Er, Ce, Li, Zn, Sn would be especially useful.

2. FINE POWDER ADDED TO MOLTEN ALUMINIUM: WETTING AND ENTRAPMENT. What is known about the difficulty of
   incorporating fine (<45 um) elemental metal or ceramic powders into molten Al — floating on the oxide
   skin, agglomeration, poor wetting, entrapment of the powder's own oxide film, and the resulting
   inclusions? Is pre-encapsulation in aluminium (foil, can, compact) a recognised mitigation? How does
   this compare with the alternative of using coarse granules or master-alloy chunks?

3. MELT-IN-PLACE / IN-SITU ALLOYING FROM A BLENDED OR ENCAPSULATED CHARGE. Evidence on making small
   experimental alloy batches (10-500 g) by melting a blended elemental/master-alloy charge in one step
   for atomization (ultrasonic atomization, gas atomization, plasma rotating electrode, suction casting,
   arc melting). What compositional accuracy, homogeneity and inclusion content are achieved? Are
   remelting / double-melting / stirring steps required before atomization?

4. GRAPHITE CRUCIBLES AND MOLTEN ALUMINIUM. Quantitative data on the reaction between molten Al (and
   Al alloys containing Ti, Zr, Sc, Li, Mg) and graphite: Al4C3 formation rate versus temperature and
   hold time, wetting/infiltration of porous graphite by Al, carbon pickup in the melt, formation of
   TiC/ZrC/Al4C3 inclusions, and the effect of carbide inclusions on LPBF powder and on Al3(Sc,Zr,Er)
   L1_2 precipitation. What crucible materials and coatings (boron nitride, alumina, yttria, zirconia,
   clay-graphite, SiC-graphite, glassy carbon) are recommended for holding Al melts at 800-1100 C, and
   how effective are BN or alumina wash coatings at suppressing Al4C3? Is lithium- or magnesium-bearing
   Al especially aggressive to oxide crucibles?

5. DOES THE ALUMINIUM CUP HELP OR HURT AT THE CRUCIBLE INTERFACE? Would a solid aluminium liner or cup
   inside a graphite crucible reduce or increase contact-time-related contamination, and what happens to
   the oxide skin of the aluminium cup itself when it melts (does it form a residual bag/oxide film that
   traps the charge)? Any literature on "sacrificial container" or "charge canister" melting practice.

6. HEATING SEQUENCE. If reactive or high-melting solute powders (Ti, Zr, Cr, Fe, Ni) are inside an
   aluminium container that melts at 660 C, what are the risks of the powders sintering, oxidising or
   forming intermetallic shells before the aluminium melts, and what heating rate/stirring practice
   (electromagnetic stirring, superheat, hold time) is recommended for complete dissolution?

Where the literature is silent, say so explicitly rather than extrapolating.

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions

        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation

    InterventionalAssignment:

    ObservationalModel:

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):

Use the tools to answer the question: We are building an automated alloy-discovery workflow that makes ~100 g batches of experimental
aluminium alloys by ULTRASONIC ATOMIZATION (AMAZEMET rePOWDER-class: induction heating, ceramic/graphite
crucible, argon atmosphere <50 ppm O2, melt dripped onto a vibrating sonotrode) to produce LPBF feedstock
powder. Alloys are Al-based with additions of Mn, Cr, Zr, Mg, Si, Cu, Ti, Fe, Ni, Ce, Sc, Li, Er, Zn, Sn
at up to a few wt.% each.

We are considering a specific charging strategy and need the literature evidence for and against it:
INSTEAD of dosing aluminium powder, we would machine or form a small CUP / CRUCIBLE / CAPSULE OUT OF
HIGH-PURITY SOLID ALUMINIUM, robotically dispense only the NON-ALUMINIUM elemental and master-alloy
POWDERS into that aluminium cup, and then place the whole loaded aluminium cup inside the atomizer's
GRAPHITE (or ceramic) CRUCIBLE and melt it. The aluminium cup is sacrificial: it becomes the base metal
of the alloy. Please address, with citations and quantitative data wherever possible:

1. ALUMINIUM ENCAPSULATION OF ALLOY ADDITIONS. Is wrapping/encapsulating alloying elements, master alloys
   or elemental powders in aluminium (Al foil packets, Al cans, compacted Al-clad briquettes, "cored wire"
   with an aluminium sheath) an established practice for adding solutes to aluminium melts? What is the
   measured effect on RECOVERY / assimilation yield of the addition, on oxidation loss, and on dross
   formation, compared with adding loose powder to an open melt? Quantitative recovery percentages for
   elements such as Mg, Mn, Cr, Ti, Zr, Sc, Er, Ce, Li, Zn, Sn would be especially useful.

2. FINE POWDER ADDED TO MOLTEN ALUMINIUM: WETTING AND ENTRAPMENT. What is known about the difficulty of
   incorporating fine (<45 um) elemental metal or ceramic powders into molten Al — floating on the oxide
   skin, agglomeration, poor wetting, entrapment of the powder's own oxide film, and the resulting
   inclusions? Is pre-encapsulation in aluminium (foil, can, compact) a recognised mitigation? How does
   this compare with the alternative of using coarse granules or master-alloy chunks?

3. MELT-IN-PLACE / IN-SITU ALLOYING FROM A BLENDED OR ENCAPSULATED CHARGE. Evidence on making small
   experimental alloy batches (10-500 g) by melting a blended elemental/master-alloy charge in one step
   for atomization (ultrasonic atomization, gas atomization, plasma rotating electrode, suction casting,
   arc melting). What compositional accuracy, homogeneity and inclusion content are achieved? Are
   remelting / double-melting / stirring steps required before atomization?

4. GRAPHITE CRUCIBLES AND MOLTEN ALUMINIUM. Quantitative data on the reaction between molten Al (and
   Al alloys containing Ti, Zr, Sc, Li, Mg) and graphite: Al4C3 formation rate versus temperature and
   hold time, wetting/infiltration of porous graphite by Al, carbon pickup in the melt, formation of
   TiC/ZrC/Al4C3 inclusions, and the effect of carbide inclusions on LPBF powder and on Al3(Sc,Zr,Er)
   L1_2 precipitation. What crucible materials and coatings (boron nitride, alumina, yttria, zirconia,
   clay-graphite, SiC-graphite, glassy carbon) are recommended for holding Al melts at 800-1100 C, and
   how effective are BN or alumina wash coatings at suppressing Al4C3? Is lithium- or magnesium-bearing
   Al especially aggressive to oxide crucibles?

5. DOES THE ALUMINIUM CUP HELP OR HURT AT THE CRUCIBLE INTERFACE? Would a solid aluminium liner or cup
   inside a graphite crucible reduce or increase contact-time-related contamination, and what happens to
   the oxide skin of the aluminium cup itself when it melts (does it form a residual bag/oxide film that
   traps the charge)? Any literature on "sacrificial container" or "charge canister" melting practice.

6. HEATING SEQUENCE. If reactive or high-melting solute powders (Ti, Zr, Cr, Fe, Ni) are inside an
   aluminium container that melts at 660 C, what are the risks of the powders sintering, oxidising or
   forming intermetallic shells before the aluminium melts, and what heating rate/stirring practice
   (electromagnetic stirring, superheat, hold time) is recommended for complete dissolution?

Bio-integrated wearable systems can measure a broad range of biophysical, biochemical, and environmental signals to provide critical insights into overall health status and to quantify human performance. Recent advances in material science, chemical analysis techniques, device designs, and assembly methods form the foundations for a uniquely differentiated type of wearable technology, characterized by noninvasive, intimate integration with the soft, curved, time-dynamic surfaces of the body. This review summarizes the latest advances in this emerging field of "bio-integrated" technologies in a comprehensive manner that connects fundamental developments in chemistry, material science, and engineering with sensing technologies that have the potential for widespread deployment and societal benefit in human health care. An introduction to the chemistries and materials for the active components of these systems contextualizes essential design considerations for sensors and associated platforms that appear in following sections. The subsequent content highlights the most advanced biosensors, classified according to their ability to capture biophysical, biochemical, and environmental information. Additional sections feature schemes for electrically powering these sensors and strategies for achieving fully integrated, wireless systems. The review concludes with an overview of key remaining challenges and a summary of opportunities where advances in materials chemistry will be critically important for continued progress.

Abstract:
Bioresorbable metals and metal alloys are of growing interest for myriad uses in temporary biomedical implants. Examples range from structural elements as stents, screws, and scaffolds to electronic components as sensors, electrical stimulators, and programmable fluidics. The associated physical forms span mechanically machined bulk parts to lithographically patterned conductive traces, across a diversity of metals and alloys based on magnesium, zinc, iron, tungsten, and others. The result is a rich set of opportunities in healthcare materials science and engineering. This review article summarizes recent advances in this area, starting with an historical perspective followed by a discussion of materials options, considerations in biocompatibility, and device applications. Highlights are in system level bioresorbable electronic platforms that support functions as diagnostics and therapeutics in the context of specific, temporary clinical needs. A concluding section highlights challenges and emerging research directions.

Abstract:
Nanomaterials are materials with one or more nanoscale dimensions (internal or external) (i.e., 1 to 100 nm). The nanomaterial shape, size, porosity, surface chemistry, and composition are controlled at the nanoscale, and this offers interesting properties compared with bulk materials. This review describes how nanomaterials are classified, their fabrication, functionalization techniques, and growth-controlled mechanisms. First, the history of nanomaterials is summarized and then the different classification methods, based on their dimensionality (0–3D), composition (carbon, inorganic, organic, and hybrids), origin (natural, incidental, engineered, bioinspired), crystal phase (single phase, multiphase), and dispersion state (dispersed or aggregated), are presented. Then, the synthesis methods are discussed and classified in function of the starting material (bottom-up and top-down), reaction phase (gas, plasma, liquid, and solid), and nature of the dispersing forces (mechanical, physical, chemical, physicochemical, and biological). Finally, the challenges in synthesizing nanomaterials for research and commercial use are highlighted.

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) of biomedical materials provides enormous opportunities to fabricate multifunctional and structurally designed frameworks for tissue engineering, such as dental implants and bone substitutes. Despite several advantages of the binder jet 3D printing technology over other AM methods, for example, no limitations in materials selection, high materials recycling efficiency, no thermal stress development, no need to support materials, and the possibility of fabrication of printing functionally graded materials, the fabrication of biomedical-grade titanium alloys with high-density, fine microstructure, and low pickup of impurities is still challenging. This work presents the effects of powder particle size and 3D printing conditions on the microstructural features and mechanical properties of Ti-6Al-4V alloy. The formation of large and inter-aggregate pores during binder jetting is demonstrated and discussed. Design and selection of particle size distribution with a mean diameter of ~20 μm and large span and positive skewness are proposed to minimize binder-induced powder aggregation and fabricate green parts with a density of 65±1% PFD (pore-free density). Dilatometric studies under a partial pressure of argon (0.1 bar) determine that sintering just above the α/β transus temperature (~980 °C) provides a high strain rate to remove pores, but high-temperature sintering (≥1250 °C) is required to attain 97% PFD. The successful fabrication of high-density Ti-6Al-4V parts (≥96% PFD) with the microstructure comparable to metal injection molding (MIM) titanium parts (≈100 μm α grains + β lattes) is demonstrated. The tensile strength and elongation values fall in the range of 880±50 MPa and 6±2% (depending on the processing condition), which is comparable with metal injection molded parts and superior to the laser powder bed fusion technology concerning ductility. The content of carbon (<0.02 wt.%) and nitrogen (0.01 wt.%) also falls in the standard region of metal injection molding. However, oxygen pickup during sintering moderately increases the oxygen content (for 30–50%) over the standard level. The concentration of interstitials entrapped in the metal is comparable to that of parts manufactured by the powder bed fusion process, but the mechanical properties are better matched with the commercial titanium alloy. The fabrication of the titanium alloy as per the ASTM F2885 standard provides an excellent opportunity for the binder jetting process to develop custom-made biomaterials.

Abstract:

 This research presents a methodology for the recycling process via casting, in which aluminum cans and primary (commercial) aluminum are transformed into a laminated tape, with the possibility of industrial application. This research was classified as bibliographic, exploratory, and experimental, since it used qualitative techniques to evaluate alternative materials. Its objective was to incorporate materials of different properties that could favor the making of a tape to be laminated. In the first casting, a recycled aluminum ingot was formed only with aluminum from beverage cans and had a material yield of 51%. In a second casting, commercial aluminum was added to the recycled aluminum ingot. After the casting process with the two cast materials, the ingot had a yield of 90%. A third casting was conducted together with the aluminum that was already formed by the ingot (50% recycled and 50% commercial). The purpose of this ingot was to incorporate other materials that could provide some characteristics, such as malleability and conductivity. The third casting was made from the second ingot, and incorporated copper and magnesium. For the design of the laminated tape, a cast was made to receive the molten aluminum from the third casting. The aluminum was cast into this mold and three tapes were produced, one with a thickness of 2 mm, another with a thickness of 3 mm and the last with a thickness of 4 mm. With these tapes, the objective was to laminate them in order to reduce their thickness to values ​​close to 0.5 mm. The casting process of aluminum cans with the addition of commercial aluminum, plus the incorporation of copper and magnesium, demonstrated facilities for thickness reduction in the process of making laminated tapes.

Abstract:
Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) have a wide range of applications from electronic products to electric mobility and space exploration rovers. This results in an increase in the demand for LIBs, driven primarily by the growth in the number of electric vehicles (EVs). This growing demand will eventually lead to large amounts of waste LIBs dumped into landfills which can cause serious environmental problems. To reduce this environmental impact, the need for efficient recycling technology emerges. Furthermore, it has been proven that recycling waste LIBs consume less material and energy than producing new ones from virgin materials. Therefore, this paper aims to review different recycling technologies including hydrometallurgy, pyrometallurgy, direct recycling, and precise separation. The review concludes that hydrometallurgy might be the most efficient method of recycling waste LIBs on an industrial scale.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>High-performance Al-based components with structural-functional integration are essential in modern industry, spanning lightweight designs, energy-efficient systems, and sustainable engineering solutions. In recent years, additive manufacturing (AM) of Al alloys and Al matrix composites (AMCs) has gained significant attraction in advanced engineering due to its potential for high performance and near-net-shape fabrication. Substantial scientific and commercial progress has yielded new AM-suitable advanced alloys and AMCs. This paper provides a dedicated review focusing on recent advances in advanced Al-based materials, particularly their material design strategies and high-value-added applications. This review first outlines Al-based materials and their AM opportunities, then comprehensively surveys recent progress in developing AMed Al alloys, including high-performance Al-Si alloys by processing control, modified wrought Al alloys and tailored Al alloys for AM. Furthermore, recent advances in AM of ceramic-particle-reinforced AMCs have been highlighted, emphasizing the pivotal role of reinforcements in enhancing printability and their influence on microstructural, mechanical, and functional characteristics. Industrial applications of AMed Al-based structures in high-end products are also presented. The review provides state-of-the-art knowledge on developing and applying high-performance Al-based materials by AM and discusses current challenges and future opportunities for advancing AM of these materials.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing (AM) has experienced exponential growth over the past two decades and now stands on the cusp of a transformative paradigm shift into the realm of multi-functional component manufacturing, known as multi-material AM (MMAM). While progress in MMAM has been more gradual compared to single-material AM, significant strides have been made in exploring the scientific and technological possibilities of this emerging field. Researchers have conducted feasibility studies and investigated various processes for multi-material deposition, encompassing polymeric, metallic, and bio-materials. To facilitate further advancements, this review paper addresses the pressing need for a consolidated document on MMAM that can serve as a comprehensive guide to the state of the art. Previous reviews have tended to focus on specific processes or materials, overlooking the overall picture of MMAM. Thus, this pioneering review endeavors to synthesize the collective knowledge and provide a holistic understanding of the multiplicity of materials and multiscale processes employed in MMAM. The review commences with an analysis of the implications of multiplicity, delving into its advantages, applications, challenges, and issues. Subsequently, it offers a detailed examination of MMAM with respect to processes, materials, capabilities, scales, and structural aspects. Seven standard AM processes and hybrid AM processes are thoroughly scrutinized in the context of their adaptation for MMAM, accompanied by specific examples, merits, and demerits. The scope of the review encompasses material combinations in polymers, composites, metals-ceramics, metal alloys, and biomaterials. Furthermore, it explores MMAM’s capabilities in fabricating bi-metallic structures and functionally/compositionally graded materials, providing insights into various scale and structural aspects. The review culminates by outlining future research directions in MMAM and offering an overall outlook on the vast potential of multiplicity in this field. By presenting a comprehensive and integrated perspective, this paper aims to catalyze further breakthroughs in MMAM, thus propelling the next generation of multi-functional component manufacturing to new heights by capitalizing on the unprecedented possibilities of MMAM.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This review compiles and analyzes the current state of the art of modified high entropy alloys (MHEAs) processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), establishing composition-processing-microstructure-property relationships that define their printability, structural integrity, and performance. After contextualizing HEA/MHEA concepts and LPBF‑specific solidification phenomena, the review places particular emphasis on the modification strategies that tailor phase stability, melt‑pool behavior, and processability. These include targeted alloying additions, principal‑element ratio adjustments, and microalloying routes to stabilize FCC/BCC/B2 phase composition, mitigate cracking, and enable precipitation strengthening or microstructural refinement under LPBF’s rapid thermal cycles. A second major focus is the correlation between these compositional modifications and the resulting mechanical properties in both the as‑built and post‑processed conditions. The compiled data reveals distinct strength-ductility regimes across Cantor‑type alloys, Al‑containing dual‑phase systems, and refractory BCC‑based MHEAs, demonstrating how specific elemental additions, phase engineering strategies, and post‑processing treatments modulate hardness, tensile behavior, elongation, and failure modes. The comparative analysis highlights the strong dependency of mechanical properties on controlled phase fractions, segregation behavior, precipitates distribution, and defects. Overall, this review shows that the successful deployment of LPBF‑processed MHEAs critically depends on composition‑aware process design, where alloy modification strategies and mechanical property requirements must be jointly optimized.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Les composites a matrices metalliques (CMM) ont interesse l'industrie de l'aluminium (Al- AI2O3, Al-SiC) a cause de la superiorite de leurs propriete mecaniques comparee a celles d'alliage d'aluminium. Les composites d'aluminium-BziC (CMM) sont devenue importante pour l'industrie de l'aluminium a cause de leurs utilisations dans des applications de haute performance telles que le stockage de rejets nucleaires radioactifs, les avions et les structures aerospatiales, dues a leur capacite d'absorber des neutrons, leur legerete, leur haute resistance et leur rigidite. La production des matrices metalliques (CMM) de B4C- aluminium n'est pas une tâche facile a cause de la faible mouillabilite de B4C par l'aluminium. De plus, B4C n'est pas stable quand il est en contact avec l'aluminium. Les analyses de l'interface basees sur la microscopie optique et la microscopie electronique a balayage ont indique la formation des particules d'A^BC et d'AlB2 autour de la particule de B4C. Cette reaction est incessante et elle a comme consequence l'epuisement de la concentration de B4C, la diminution de la fluidite de la fonte et la deterioration de ses proprietes mecaniques et physiques. Pour empecher la perte de B4C, le Ti est ajoute a l'aluminium. Le Ti a de l'affinite a reagir avec B4C et forme une couche protectrice autour de la particule. 
 
Les objectifs du projet sont d'etudier la mouillabilite des systemes B4C/aluminium et B4C/alliage d'aluminium-titane et d'identifier d'autres elements d'alliage potentiels pour proteger B4C. Les experiences de mouillabiiite sont effectuees pour mesurer les angles de contact de B4C aussi bien que ceux des produits de reaction entre les elements d'alliage et B4C. Aussi, l'effet de la teneur en Ti de l'aluminium sur la mouillabilite de B4C a etem etudie. 
 
Les resultats des experiences montrent que l'addition de titane et de zirconium a l'aluminium a un effet positif fort sur le mouillage entre les particules de B4C et le metal liquide. Afin de comprendre les effets que la reaction produit sur la mouillabilite, les angles de contact entre les produits de la reaction (particules de TiC, T1B2, AIB2 and AI4C3) et l'aluminium ont ete mesures a 750°C et 850°C. Les resultats demontrent egalement que la mouillabilite de B4C augmente avec la temperature et le temps de contact. 
 
On a constate que les particules de l'Alle disparaissent avec l'addition de Ti et de nouvelles particules en forme d'aiguille (T1B2) riches en Ti se forment autour des particules de B4C. Celles-ci agissent comme une barriere qui isole le B4C de la matrice d'aluminium. On observe egalement que la formation d'A^BC diminue avec l'augmentation de la teneur en Ti. Cependant, si on continue d'augmenter la teneur en Ti, des plaques intermetalliques d'AOTi se forment ce qui reduit la mouillabilite. Cette etude a demontre qu'il y a une teneur en Ti optimale ou le mouillage est le meilleur. Cette valeur semble etre autour de 1.5%Ti. L'augmentation de la teneur en Ti au dela de cette concentration deteriore le mouillage. L'aluminium est une des industries principales au Canada et au Quebec, et les resultats de cette etude aideront a ameliorer la qualite du produit grâce au transfert de la technologie vers l'industrie.

Abstract:
Selective laser melting (SLM) in situ alloying is an effective way to design and fabricate novel materials in which the elemental powder is adopted as the raw material and micro-areas of elemental powder blend are alloyed synchronously in the forming process of selective laser melting (SLM). The pre-alloying process of preparation of raw material powder can be left out, and a batch of bulk samples can be prepared via the technology combined with quantitative powder mixing and feeding. The technique can be applied to high-throughput sample preparation to efficiently obtain a microstructure and performance data for material design. In the present work, bulk equiatomic FeCoCrNi high-entropy alloys with different processing parameters were fabricated via laser in situ alloying. Finite element simulation and CALPHAD calculation were used to determine the appropriate SLM and post-heating parameters. SEM (scanning electron microscope), EDS (energy dispersive spectroscopy), XRD (X-ray diffraction), and mechanical testing were used to characterize the composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties of as-printed and post-heat-treated samples. The experimental results show that the composition deviation of laser in situ alloying samples could be controlled within 20 wt %. The crystal structure of as-printed samples is a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC), which is the same as those prepared by the traditional method. The mechanical properties of the samples prepared by laser in situ alloying with elemental powder blend are comparable to those prepared by pre-alloying powder and much higher than those prepared by the traditional method (arc melting). As-printed samples can get a homogeneous microstructure under the optimal laser in situ alloying process combined with post-heat treatment at 1200 °C for 20 h.

Abstract:
Double oxide films (bifilms) are significant defects in the casting of light alloys, and have been shown to decrease tensile and fatigue properties, and also increase their scatter, making casting properties unreproducible and unreliable. Recent research has suggested that the nature of oxide film defects may change with time, as the air inside the bifilm would react with the surrounding melt leading to its consumption, which may enhance the mechanical properties of Al alloy castings. It was suggested that in a pure Al melt, oxygen within the bifilm atmosphere would be consumed first to form alumina, then nitrogen would react to from AlN. A CFD model of the heat distribution associated with the reactions between the interior atmosphere of a double oxide film defect and the surrounding liquid alloy suggested that highly localized increases in temperature, up to 5000, could occur, over a scale of a few hundred micrometers. Such localized increases in temperature might lead to change the nature of the bifilm causing it to be less harmful to the properties of Al cast alloys.

Abstract:
This paper presents a personal view by the author of the role of bifilms in Al alloys. The mantra ‘microstructure determines properties’ is widely accepted as a truism, but is here critically assessed and found wanting. The case is made that bifilms from the casting process, while often invisible in the microstructure, are usually at least as important, if not of far greater importance, because they are often present as a dense population of cracks throughout the metal. The bifilm population controls the morphology of many features of cast and wrought structures. For cast alloys, bifilm control of pore morphology and Si morphology in Al–Si alloys is discussed, as is dendrite arm spacing (DAS). The tensile property benefits of grain refinement are seen to be mainly bifilm controlled. The properties ductility and fatigue appear to be especially dominated by bifilm content, as are invasive corrosion processes such as pitting, intergranular corrosion, hydrogen blistering and cracking. Bifilm control is proposed as a new concept permitting the improvement and control of metallurgical properties.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>High-aluminum refractory compositionally complex alloys are intrinsically brittle due to ordering and grain-boundary intermetallics. We show that extreme thermal gradients during selective laser melting kinetically suppress these transformations in NbMoCrTiAl, stabilizing a disordered A2 solid solution despite strong thermodynamic driving forces for B2 ordering and C14/A15 formation. Multi-scale characterization and kinetic simulations reveal how rapid liquid-solid and solid-state transformations dissolve intermetallic phases and prevent reordering during cooling. The resulting precipitate-free A2 microstructure exhibits substantially enhanced room-temperature plasticity, overcoming brittleness without compositional modification. Our results establish non-equilibrium processing as a route to access otherwise inaccessible phase states in refractory complex alloys, expanding the design space of high-temperature structural materials.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Rotary furnaces remain important in secondary aluminum production because they can process oxidized, coated, low-density, contaminated, and dross-rich feeds that are difficult to recover in conventional bath furnaces. Their flexibility creates a recovery–residue trade-off: heat, rotation, and chloride–fluoride fluxes can liberate and coalesce metal droplets, but may also increase oxidation, emissions, refractory attack, and salt-slag generation. This structured critical narrative review evaluates a coded corpus of 106 publications from 2020 to August 2026. Retrospective A–E classification was performed by one reviewer and represents interpretive judgments of industrial transferability. No level-A repeated industrial campaign with closed aluminum–salt–energy–quality balances was identified. Accordingly, the proposed nine-gate Feedstock–Flux–Furnace–Residue framework is a testable decision architecture rather than a validated control model; low-salt and salt-free strategies remain feed-specific and require prospective industrial validation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In recent years, many alloys as well as composites of aluminium were developed for enhanced material performance. AA 6061 is an aluminium alloy that has extensive applications due to its superior material characteristics. It is a popular choice of matrix for aluminium matrix composite (AMC) fabrication. This study provides a review on AA 6061 aluminium alloy matrix composites produced through the stir-casting process. It focusses on conventional stir-casting fabrication, process parameters, various reinforcements used, and the mechanical properties of the AA 6061 composites. Several research studies indicated that the stir-casting method is widely used and suitable for fabricating AA 6061 composites with reinforcements such as SiC, B4C, Al2O3, TiC, as well as other inorganic, organic, hybrid, and nanomaterials. The majority of the studies showed that an increase in the reinforcement content enhanced the mechanical and tribological properties of the composites. Furthermore, hybrid composites showed better material properties than single reinforcement composites. The usage of industrial and agricultural residues in hybrid composites is also reported. Future studies could focus on the fabrication of AA 6061 nanocomposites through stir casting and their material characterisation, since they have great potential as advanced materials.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'sarkar2009investigationonwetting pages 41-46'.

Arunima Sarkar. Investigation on wetting of b4c by aluminum alloys. ArXiv, Jan 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1522/030134460, doi:10.1522/030134460. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt identifies several mechanisms relevant to incorporating fine ceramic powders into molten aluminium, but it does not specifically compare wrapping particles in aluminium foil with adding master-alloy chunks. Fine powders become increasingly difficult to disperse as particle size decreases because their larger specific surface area promotes agglomeration or clumping. Excessive particle size or microscale roughness can hinder liquid-metal spreading, reduce wettability, and create fracture-initiation sites near the interface. Particle surfaces are commonly covered by a gas layer that prevents molten aluminium from contacting the ceramic; at sufficiently high particle concentration, these layers may bridge and cause total rejection of particles from the melt. The text therefore emphasizes desorbing gases by heat treatment or breaking gas layers mechanically before synthesis. Poor wetting also affects particle position: particles that become completely wetted may sink rather than float, while inadequate wetting can promote rejection or entrapment at the melt surface. Oxide films on molten-metal droplets can mask the true wetting behavior; high temperature may degrade the oxide skin and allow metal penetration, while controlled vacuum or purified atmospheres are used to reduce oxidation. The excerpt discusses coatings, particle treatment, and alloying additions as general wetting-promotion methods, but provides no direct evidence about foil wrapping or master-alloy-chunk processing.

## pqac-00000003

From text 'kumar2024investigationofaluminum pages 4-7'.

P Kumar, D Kumar, and K Kaur. Investigation of aluminum metal matrix composite fabrication processes: a comparative review. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt describes incorporating fine reinforcement particles into molten aluminium primarily through stir casting. Aluminium is melted at approximately 700–800 °C, and a mechanical stirrer creates a vortex. Preheated particles such as SiC or Al2O3 are introduced slowly into this vortex, then the slurry is stirred for a specified duration to promote dispersion. Preheating is important because it limits excessive cooling of the melt and improves wetting and bonding between the particles and aluminium. Degassing may subsequently be used to remove trapped gases and reduce porosity. The text also emphasizes that particle size, shape, and behaviour strongly affect composite quality; smaller particles can improve mechanical properties, but achieving uniform distribution is important. Related infiltration processing uses pressure or vacuum to overcome molten aluminium’s surface tension, improve penetration into a porous reinforcement, and minimize voids. The excerpt identifies the general risks associated with inadequate processing—poor wetting, nonuniform dispersion, porosity, and voids—but it does not specifically discuss particle floating, oxide-skin effects, particle agglomeration mechanisms, or entrapment in detail. It also provides no comparison between wrapping particles in aluminium foil and adding master-alloy chunks; therefore, conclusions about the relative effectiveness of those two techniques are not supported by this passage.

## pqac-00000004

From text 'kumar2024investigationofaluminum pages 7-10'.

P Kumar, D Kumar, and K Kaur. Investigation of aluminum metal matrix composite fabrication processes: a comparative review. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt describes incorporating fine reinforcement powders into molten aluminium through a two-step stir-casting process. Reinforcement particles are preheated—typically at 200–500 °C for 30–60 minutes—to remove moisture and undesirable gases and to improve wetting with the aluminium. They are then introduced into the molten or semi-solid slurry while mechanical stirring creates a vortex, enabling the particles to enter and disperse through the melt. The slurry is reheated to full liquidity, mixed, and poured into a mould while avoiding premature solidification. Dispersion depends on particle injection rate, wetting, porosity, stirrer design, blade angle, stirring speed and duration, degassing, and solidification conditions. Poor wetting, associated with high contact angle or interfacial tension, can cause non-uniform dispersion, weak interfacial bonding, reduced homogeneity, and inferior mechanical properties. Excessive feeding rates promote particle agglomeration; the excerpt identifies 8–10 mg/min as a reported effective rate. Particle settling during heating and solidification is also a major concern, while porosity and entrapped gases degrade performance. Vortex formation, purging/degassing, controlled pouring, and mould preheating address these issues. The provided pages do not discuss aluminium-foil wrapping, floating specifically, oxide-skin effects, or comparisons with master-alloy chunks.

The excerpt provides partial guidance on incorporating fine particulate material into molten aluminium, mainly by describing the interfacial and mixing mechanisms required for recovery. Fine chips, foils, and powders are difficult because their exposed surface area is large relative to their metal inventory, making them especially vulnerable to oxidation and oxide-film formation during heating and stirring. For metal to incorporate successfully, particles or droplets must become exposed, collide with other metal, drain the intervening oxide or liquid film, and coalesce before they are immobilized in cooling slag. Poor wetting and persistent oxide envelopes hinder this sequence; salt chemistry can modify oxide wetting, interfacial tension, viscosity, and film disruption. Fluoride-bearing fluxes may improve refining and coalescence but create corrosion, volatile-fluoride, and water-treatment concerns. Mixing is also critical: inadequate rotation leaves unmixed regions and entrapped droplets, whereas moderate rotation renews particle–metal contact. The excerpt reports foil compaction as a preparation variable and notes that oxidation decreased above approximately 2.4 g cm⁻³, with 99–100% recovery reported for compacted 15 μm foil under controlled laboratory conditions. It does not provide a direct comparison between aluminium-foil wrapping and master-alloy chunks, nor detailed evidence specifically on floating or agglomeration.

## pqac-00000007

From text 'dispinar2006determinationofmetal pages 20-23'.

D Dispinar. Determination of metal quality of aluminium and its alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt does not specifically describe how fine powders or particles should be incorporated into molten aluminium, nor does it compare direct addition with wrapping particles in aluminium foil or using master-alloy chunks. It does, however, identify the melt-handling mechanisms that are highly relevant to such additions. Aluminium melts readily absorb hydrogen, which becomes much less soluble during solidification and can produce gas porosity. Oxide films form inevitably at exposed liquid-aluminium surfaces; if surface films are folded into the melt, they can trap gas and become double-oxide-film (bifilm) defects. Oxides may enter from the charge during melting and may be further introduced by poor handling, especially violent stirring or pouring. These inclusions act as stress raisers, while gas and shrinkage porosity make casting properties unpredictable and can reduce ductility and fatigue performance. The passage therefore supports the conclusion that any particle-addition technique must minimize surface disturbance, oxide entrainment, and hydrogen pickup. It provides no direct evidence about particle wetting, agglomeration, floating, foil dissolution, or the comparative effectiveness of master-alloy chunks; those issues would require additional source material.

The excerpt does not specifically describe techniques for incorporating fine powders or particles into molten aluminium, nor does it compare aluminium-foil wrapping with the addition of master-alloy chunks. It does, however, identify mechanisms and defect risks relevant to particle addition. Molten aluminium rapidly forms an oxide surface film, and surface folding or disturbance can push that film into the melt. When two non-wetting oxide surfaces meet with gas trapped between them, they form a double oxide-film defect (bifilm), which behaves like a crack. Poor wetting and agglomeration would therefore be relevant because they can promote folded or entrained oxide films and prevent effective dispersion, although these particular particle-processing effects are not developed in the excerpt. Hydrogen is another major concern: moisture in fluxes, crucibles, refractories, charge materials, or humid air reacts with aluminium to generate hydrogen. Hydrogen becomes less soluble as the alloy cools, potentially precipitating as gas and producing porosity. The passage also indicates that oxide-film behavior changes with time and temperature, from thin “young oxides” to thicker crystalline “old oxides,” while oxide transformations can cause fracture and breakaway oxidation. No evidence is provided here regarding floating particles, foil wrapping, or master-alloy chunk performance.

To decouple the synergistic effects of Cu and Si alloying elements and VED, Ti-5Cu-1Si and pure Ti were further printed at a consistent VED of 43.98 J/mm³. Incorporating Cu and Si into pure Ti induced a grain morphology shift from columnar prior β to equiaxed β grain morphology. Elevating the VED beyond 43.98 J/mm³ promoted a dense population of equiaxed prior β grains, reducing the average grain size from 4.723 µm to 1.922 µm and markedly improving grain size uniformity. On the other hand, increasing VED from 43.98 to 77.55 J/mm³ was accompanied by an increase in the β phase fraction from 22.59 to 37.06% at the expense of a reduction in the α phase fraction from 23.63 to 8.08%. The slower cooling rate associated with the highest VED of 77.55 J/mm³ promoted the diffusion of supersaturated Cu and Si atoms out of the Ti lattice, thereby reducing lattice microstrain from 0.46% to 0.16%. The electrochemical results highlighted that a set of microstructural evolution and enhanced microstructural homogenization induced by elevated VED manifest as a promotion of the corrosion potential ( E corr ) from − 0.26 V to -0.17 V and a concomitantly decline in corrosion current density ( I corr ) from 7.86 µA/cm 2 to 1.43 µA/cm 2 . These microstructural evolutions, coupled with favorable electrochemical responses, were demonstrably associated with an increase in the average passive film resistance ( R p ) on Ti-5Cu-1Si alloy, enhancing from 9.2 KΩ. cm 2 up to 11.53 KΩ. cm 2 .

## pqac-00000010

From text 'dispinar2006determinationofmetal pages 20-23'.

D Dispinar. Determination of metal quality of aluminium and its alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt presents the bifilm as a double oxide-film defect formed when an oxide-covered aluminium melt surface folds over and traps gas between two non-wetting oxide layers. The resulting folded film behaves like a crack within the liquid metal. Oxide contamination begins during melting: when solid aluminium charge or scrap is submerged and melts, its surface oxide can detach, float free, and become suspended in the melt. The excerpt indicates that these oxides may subsequently appear in castings as massive, film-like, dross-like, or other non-metallic inclusions. However, simple detachment and suspension are distinct from true bifilm entrainment; additional oxide is incorporated when the melt is handled violently, stirred, poured, or otherwise disturbed, causing surface films to be folded into the liquid with trapped gas. Such defects are stress-raisers and, together with hydrogen-related gas porosity and shrinkage porosity, can make casting properties unpredictable. They can significantly reduce or affect mechanical performance, particularly ductility and fatigue properties, and may cause premature component failure. Consequently, the excerpt identifies melt control and careful, quiescent handling during melting and pouring as central to aluminium casting quality.


---

## pqac-00000011

From text 'dispinar2006determinationofmetal pages 12-16'.

D Dispinar. Determination of metal quality of aluminium and its alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt presents bifilms as entrained aluminium-oxide defects formed during melting and melt handling. An oxide film on molten aluminium can become folded or doubled over during turbulent handling, trapping an air gap; this creates a planar, crack-like inclusion that may remain in the melt and be carried into the casting. The passage does not explicitly confirm that the oxide skin already present on every solid charge or scrap piece necessarily becomes a bifilm, but it identifies entrained oxide generated or incorporated during melting and handling as a major source of melt-quality defects. Bifilms are particularly important because dissolved hydrogen alone cannot nucleate porosity without such oxide surfaces. Hydrogen can enter or expand the gap between the oxide layers, producing pores, while pressure and oxidation can enlarge and stabilize the defect. Consequently, bifilms and hydrogen contribute to porosity, reduced melt cleanliness, and defects in the final microstructure. Their presence can reduce tensile strength and elongation, increase variability in mechanical properties, and impair component reliability and service life. Filters may prevent some defects from reaching the casting, but the excerpt emphasizes that quality control must begin with melt-quality control. It also notes that the conventional reduced-pressure test gives only an imperfect comparative indication because it cannot reliably separate hydrogen effects from metal cleanliness or bifilm content.

## pqac-00000012

From text 'campbell2021apersonalview pages 1-2'.

John Campbell. A personal view of microstructure and properties of al alloys. Materials, 14:1297, Mar 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma14051297, doi:10.3390/ma14051297. This article has 32 citations.

The excerpt presents a bifilm as a doubled, folded or contacting oxide layer created when separate aluminium fragments, droplets, splashes, or particles come together during consolidation or pouring. Each contributing metal surface is normally covered by oxide; when the pieces meet, the dry oxide surfaces contact one another, producing an internal interface with practically no bonding, while the outer oxide surfaces remain well wetted and bonded to the surrounding aluminium matrix. In this sense, oxide skins already present on solid charge or scrap can be understood as potential bifilm sources when oxide-covered pieces are incorporated into the melt or consolidated into cast metal. However, the excerpt does not explicitly describe the detailed remelting mechanism or quantify how much charge oxide survives as inclusions, so that specific question requires additional evidence. Bifilms act like internal cracks and may remain suspended because air trapped between oxide layers gives them nearly neutral buoyancy. Their size varies with the size of poured drops and splashes, producing statistical variability. The stated consequences include reduced mechanical properties, dense populations of internal cracks, porosity and altered pore morphology, processing failures such as slab, log, rolling, forging, and extrusion cracking, high scrap rates, and particularly impaired ductility, fatigue performance, and susceptibility to corrosion, hydrogen blistering, and cracking.

URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40962-026-02008-z, doi:10.1007/s40962-026-02008-z. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt presents the bifilm concept as the formation of double-layered oxide-film defects when an oxide-covered aluminum melt surface is disturbed and the surface oxide is folded or entrained into the liquid. The resulting defect is effectively a doubled, unbonded oxide interface, commonly associated with entrained air or bubbles. The text emphasizes that bifilms are numerous and have very high total surface area: populations of approximately 10^6–10^9 m^-3 may occur in ordinary aluminum melts, and 0.1–2.0 m^2 of oxide-film surface may be entrained per 10 kg of poured metal. Regarding solid charge or scrap, this excerpt does not directly establish that every oxide skin present on charge automatically becomes a bifilm during melting. It does support the broader conclusion that oxide skins can become entrained whenever melting, transfer, pouring, or stirring disturbs oxide-covered surfaces; whether they survive, fold, disperse, or settle depends on processing conditions. Bifilms can act as harmful casting defects, contribute to porosity and reduce melt quality, and interact with grain-refiner particles. The study also indicates that attaching dense grain-refiner particles can promote bifilm sedimentation and lower measured porosity, demonstrating that bifilm distribution strongly influences casting quality.

## pqac-00000014

From text 'yousefian2017poreformationin pages 42-47'.

P Yousefian. Pore formation in aluminum castings: theoretical calculations and the extrinsic effect of entrained surface oxide films. Unknown journal, 2017.

The bifilm concept describes the formation of internal double oxide-film defects when the surface oxide skin on liquid aluminium is submerged by surface turbulence or another external/internal force. As the skin is folded into the melt, two oxide surfaces come into contact but do not bond, leaving a thin, crack-like unbonded inclusion containing an internal interface. The excerpt specifically discusses oxide-film entrainment during melt handling and filling; it does not directly establish whether the oxide skin originally present on every solid aluminium charge or scrap piece necessarily becomes entrained bifilm inclusions during remelting. However, oxide skins can be incorporated into the melt when melt movement or turbulence folds and transports them into the bulk liquid. These bifilms are often extremely thin and difficult to detect, but they can act as initiation sites for pores and cracks. Dissolved gas, especially under reduced pressure or during solidification, can open the unbonded films and produce porosity. Consequently, entrainment can reduce casting quality, including bending strength and likely reliability, while creating defects that may remain invisible to routine inspection. The excerpt also identifies a critical surface-breaking velocity of approximately 0.35–0.5 m/s, above which surface turbulence and oxide entrainment become much more likely.

Sādhanā, Dec 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12046-024-02648-z, doi:10.1007/s12046-024-02648-z. This article has 3 citations.

The bifilm concept describes folded, doubled oxide films entrained into liquid aluminium when the melt surface is disturbed. Turbulent pouring, transfer, splashing, or surface waves can cause the oxide skin on the melt to fold inward and become submerged; the two oxide surfaces create a planar internal defect that may contain an air gap. The excerpt directly supports this mechanism for oxide films already present on the liquid-metal surface. It does not explicitly establish that the oxide skin originally present on every solid aluminium charge or scrap piece necessarily becomes a bifilm inclusion during melting. However, oxide-covered charge and scrap can plausibly contribute oxide films to the melt, particularly if they are not dissolved or removed and if melting or transfer creates turbulence. Bifilms may float or sink depending on their density and can become trapped in the solidifying casting. Their unbonded surfaces and entrapped atmosphere promote gas entrapment, gas porosity, and shrinkage porosity; oxide-wrapped inclusions contribute inclusion defects. They also act as weak internal features that can initiate crack formation and facilitate hot-tear propagation. Consequently, bifilms substantially reduce melt cleanliness and degrade casting integrity and mechanical properties, producing porosity, inclusions, cracks, and possible casting failure.
