## pqac-00000010

From text 'dispinar2006determinationofmetal pages 20-23'.

D Dispinar. Determination of metal quality of aluminium and its alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt presents the bifilm as a double oxide-film defect formed when an oxide-covered aluminium melt surface folds over and traps gas between two non-wetting oxide layers. The resulting folded film behaves like a crack within the liquid metal. Oxide contamination begins during melting: when solid aluminium charge or scrap is submerged and melts, its surface oxide can detach, float free, and become suspended in the melt. The excerpt indicates that these oxides may subsequently appear in castings as massive, film-like, dross-like, or other non-metallic inclusions. However, simple detachment and suspension are distinct from true bifilm entrainment; additional oxide is incorporated when the melt is handled violently, stirred, poured, or otherwise disturbed, causing surface films to be folded into the liquid with trapped gas. Such defects are stress-raisers and, together with hydrogen-related gas porosity and shrinkage porosity, can make casting properties unpredictable. They can significantly reduce or affect mechanical performance, particularly ductility and fatigue properties, and may cause premature component failure. Consequently, the excerpt identifies melt control and careful, quiescent handling during melting and pouring as central to aluminium casting quality.


---

## pqac-00000011

From text 'dispinar2006determinationofmetal pages 12-16'.

D Dispinar. Determination of metal quality of aluminium and its alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt presents bifilms as entrained aluminium-oxide defects formed during melting and melt handling. An oxide film on molten aluminium can become folded or doubled over during turbulent handling, trapping an air gap; this creates a planar, crack-like inclusion that may remain in the melt and be carried into the casting. The passage does not explicitly confirm that the oxide skin already present on every solid charge or scrap piece necessarily becomes a bifilm, but it identifies entrained oxide generated or incorporated during melting and handling as a major source of melt-quality defects. Bifilms are particularly important because dissolved hydrogen alone cannot nucleate porosity without such oxide surfaces. Hydrogen can enter or expand the gap between the oxide layers, producing pores, while pressure and oxidation can enlarge and stabilize the defect. Consequently, bifilms and hydrogen contribute to porosity, reduced melt cleanliness, and defects in the final microstructure. Their presence can reduce tensile strength and elongation, increase variability in mechanical properties, and impair component reliability and service life. Filters may prevent some defects from reaching the casting, but the excerpt emphasizes that quality control must begin with melt-quality control. It also notes that the conventional reduced-pressure test gives only an imperfect comparative indication because it cannot reliably separate hydrogen effects from metal cleanliness or bifilm content.


---

## pqac-00000012

From text 'campbell2021apersonalview pages 1-2'.

John Campbell. A personal view of microstructure and properties of al alloys. Materials, 14:1297, Mar 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma14051297, doi:10.3390/ma14051297. This article has 32 citations.

The excerpt presents a bifilm as a doubled, folded or contacting oxide layer created when separate aluminium fragments, droplets, splashes, or particles come together during consolidation or pouring. Each contributing metal surface is normally covered by oxide; when the pieces meet, the dry oxide surfaces contact one another, producing an internal interface with practically no bonding, while the outer oxide surfaces remain well wetted and bonded to the surrounding aluminium matrix. In this sense, oxide skins already present on solid charge or scrap can be understood as potential bifilm sources when oxide-covered pieces are incorporated into the melt or consolidated into cast metal. However, the excerpt does not explicitly describe the detailed remelting mechanism or quantify how much charge oxide survives as inclusions, so that specific question requires additional evidence. Bifilms act like internal cracks and may remain suspended because air trapped between oxide layers gives them nearly neutral buoyancy. Their size varies with the size of poured drops and splashes, producing statistical variability. The stated consequences include reduced mechanical properties, dense populations of internal cracks, porosity and altered pore morphology, processing failures such as slab, log, rolling, forging, and extrusion cracking, high scrap rates, and particularly impaired ductility, fatigue performance, and susceptibility to corrosion, hydrogen blistering, and cracking.

## pqac-00000013

From text 'gyarmati2026understandingtheinteractions pages 1-2'.

Gábor Gyarmati. Understanding the interactions of grain refiner particles and double oxide films in liquid aluminum alloys. International Journal of Metalcasting, May 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40962-026-02008-z, doi:10.1007/s40962-026-02008-z. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt presents the bifilm concept as the formation of double-layered oxide-film defects when an oxide-covered aluminum melt surface is disturbed and the surface oxide is folded or entrained into the liquid. The resulting defect is effectively a doubled, unbonded oxide interface, commonly associated with entrained air or bubbles. The text emphasizes that bifilms are numerous and have very high total surface area: populations of approximately 10^6–10^9 m^-3 may occur in ordinary aluminum melts, and 0.1–2.0 m^2 of oxide-film surface may be entrained per 10 kg of poured metal. Regarding solid charge or scrap, this excerpt does not directly establish that every oxide skin present on charge automatically becomes a bifilm during melting. It does support the broader conclusion that oxide skins can become entrained whenever melting, transfer, pouring, or stirring disturbs oxide-covered surfaces; whether they survive, fold, disperse, or settle depends on processing conditions. Bifilms can act as harmful casting defects, contribute to porosity and reduce melt quality, and interact with grain-refiner particles. The study also indicates that attaching dense grain-refiner particles can promote bifilm sedimentation and lower measured porosity, demonstrating that bifilm distribution strongly influences casting quality.

## pqac-00000014

From text 'yousefian2017poreformationin pages 42-47'.

P Yousefian. Pore formation in aluminum castings: theoretical calculations and the extrinsic effect of entrained surface oxide films. Unknown journal, 2017.

The bifilm concept describes the formation of internal double oxide-film defects when the surface oxide skin on liquid aluminium is submerged by surface turbulence or another external/internal force. As the skin is folded into the melt, two oxide surfaces come into contact but do not bond, leaving a thin, crack-like unbonded inclusion containing an internal interface. The excerpt specifically discusses oxide-film entrainment during melt handling and filling; it does not directly establish whether the oxide skin originally present on every solid aluminium charge or scrap piece necessarily becomes entrained bifilm inclusions during remelting. However, oxide skins can be incorporated into the melt when melt movement or turbulence folds and transports them into the bulk liquid. These bifilms are often extremely thin and difficult to detect, but they can act as initiation sites for pores and cracks. Dissolved gas, especially under reduced pressure or during solidification, can open the unbonded films and produce porosity. Consequently, entrainment can reduce casting quality, including bending strength and likely reliability, while creating defects that may remain invisible to routine inspection. The excerpt also identifies a critical surface-breaking velocity of approximately 0.35–0.5 m/s, above which surface turbulence and oxide entrainment become much more likely.

It does provide general guidance relevant to interpreting such measurements. Abstract:
The temperature field in welded plates has a significant influence on the microstructure and thereby their properties during friction stir welding (FSW). In this work, a self-designed heat pipe with different cooling liquid was applied in the FSW process for AZ31 magnesium alloy. The temperature fields, microstructures and properties of the welded joints were investigated. The peak temperatures and the durations of high temperature at both the advancing side and the retreating side decrease during the FSW process after applying the heat pipe and adding the ambient temperature water in the condensing tank. The top part of the weld nugget zone of the joint shows a significant decrease as well as its middle part due to the cooling effect of the heat pipe. The microstructure of the weld nugget zone is refined, associated with the increase in the hardness after applying the heat pipe. When the cooling liquid turns into ice water, grains in the weld nugget zone become significantly smaller and have a more homogeneous size. The mean value of hardness increases and the corresponding deviation is declined. Therefore, these results indicate that the application of the heat pipe and the employment of ice water as the cooling liquid can further refine the microstructure and enhance the strength of the material.

## pqac-00000030

From text 'najafabadi1996thekineticsof pages 25-28'.

A Shafyei Najafabadi. The kinetics of dissolution of high melting point alloying elements in molten aluminum. Unknown journal, 1996.

The excerpt specifically addresses manganese and iron, not titanium, zirconium, chromium, or nickel, so it does not provide their individual dissolution kinetics or intermetallic phases. For Mn–Al and Fe–Al briquettes, aluminum powder melts within the compact, after which exothermic reactions between the alloying particles and aluminum raise the briquette temperature substantially above the surrounding molten-aluminum bath. Intermetallic layers form around the alloying-element particles; based on the phase diagrams and experimental observations, MnAl4 and FeAl3 are identified as the dominant phases in the briquettes. Briquettes swell and allow molten aluminum to penetrate, so particles begin dissolving before the briquette disintegrates. The internal heat and exothermic reactions accelerate dissolution, producing a very high solute uptake immediately after disintegration. Once particles are dispersed, dissolution is controlled primarily by mass transfer from solid particles into the turbulent liquid. Stirring enhances transfer and suspension: Kolmogoroff’s approach was applicable at lower mixing-energy inputs, before full suspension. After particles became fully suspended, additional increases in mixing rate caused negligible changes in mass-transfer coefficients. The excerpt does not explicitly discuss elements wrapped in aluminum foil; its closest comparable system is aluminum-containing briquettes, whose thermal reaction, swelling, penetration, and breakup accelerate dissolution. Temperature effects are described through the briquette’s self-heating, rather than through a systematic bath-temperature study.

## pqac-00000031

From text 'najafabadi1996thekineticsof pages 33-37'.

A Shafyei Najafabadi. The kinetics of dissolution of high melting point alloying elements in molten aluminum. Unknown journal, 1996.

The excerpt provides general dissolution kinetics for high-melting-point additions, specifically iron and manganese in molten aluminum, but does not report results for Ti, Zr, Cr, or Ni, nor does it identify the intermetallic layers formed. These elements generally dissolve rather than melt. The process is described as being controlled mainly by solute mass transfer through an interfacial boundary layer, with the flux represented by Fick’s law or, under stirring, by J = Km(Cs − Cb). Low diffusivity and low solubility of Fe and Mn in aluminum make dissolution slow. Mechanical stirring or gas/impeller agitation enhances dissolution by reducing the effective concentration-boundary-layer thickness and increasing the mass-transfer coefficient. The investigation compares compact briquettes with the original discrete powders. Powders were classified by size, wrapped in aluminum foil, and plunged into molten aluminum so their dissolution times could be compared in an intensively stirred melt. The excerpt does not state what physically happens after plunging beyond describing the experimental procedure, and it gives no temperature-effect results. Separate samples were immersed at 1100°C, withdrawn at five-second intervals, rapidly quenched, and examined metallographically and by EDS to study aluminum–particle reactions and the layers formed, but the resulting layer compositions are not included here.

## pqac-00000032

From text 'najafabadi1996thekineticsof pages 37-41'.

A Shafyei Najafabadi. The kinetics of dissolution of high melting point alloying elements in molten aluminum. Unknown journal, 1996.

The excerpt directly addresses Fe and Mn dissolution in molten aluminum, while it does not provide specific kinetics for Ti, Zr, Cr, or Ni, nor does it discuss aluminum-foil wrapping or the effects of stirring and systematic temperature variation. For Fe-Al and Mn-Al briquettes, dissolution proceeds through intermetallic-layer formation rather than simple direct dissolution. Aluminum particles first melt, flow through the briquette pores, wet the alloying element, and initiate an exothermic reaction. Thick intermetallic rims form rapidly around the particles. Although several equilibrium phases are possible, Fe2Al5 is reported as the dominant Fe-Al layer and MnAl4 as the dominant Mn-Al layer; the other phases are presumed to be immeasurably thin. Growth can occur at both the intermetallic/liquid-aluminum interface and the intermetallic/solid-element interface, with both alloying-element and aluminum atoms diffusing through the layer. The briquette temperature may rise sharply above the bath temperature after aluminum melting, and the reaction can continue even after withdrawal from the melt. Ultimately, loss of rigidity and disintegration occurs; iron briquettes disintegrated after approximately 25 seconds in the cited observation.

## pqac-00000033

From text 'najafabadi1996thekineticsof pages 48-51'.

A Shafyei Najafabadi. The kinetics of dissolution of high melting point alloying elements in molten aluminum. Unknown journal, 1996.

The excerpt directly discusses Fe–Al and Mn–Al systems, rather than providing dissolution kinetics for all six requested elements (Ti, Zr, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Mn). For Fe and Mn briquettes in molten aluminum, dissolution begins rapidly—about 25–35 seconds after insertion, coinciding with briquette disintegration—under highly stirred or fully entrained conditions. Before disintegration, molten aluminum penetrates the compact and dissolves Fe or Mn into locally unsaturated liquid. Heat accumulated or released within the briquette increases liquid-side solubility and diffusion rates, producing a locally supersaturated liquid. When the briquette collapses, this solute-rich aluminum disperses into the bath and causes a sharp concentration increase. Aluminum preferentially diffuses into the solid Fe or Mn particles, causing particle growth and briquette swelling; pores form where original aluminum particles were located. Intermetallic compounds form around the alloying particles and have greater specific volume than the pure metals, further increasing expansion. The excerpt does not identify complete intermetallic-layer sequences for Ti, Zr, Cr, Fe, Ni, or Mn, nor does it specifically describe aluminum-foil-wrapped additions; the briquette behavior is the closest analogous case. Increased temperature and stirring enhance dissolution by increasing solubility, diffusion, wetting, penetration, and transport into the melt.

High-melting-point additions—explicitly including Mn, Fe, and Cr—normally dissolve in molten aluminum rather than melt. Their dissolution is generally controlled by solute mass transfer through a boundary layer between the solid addition and the bulk liquid; heat transfer is described as secondary. The solute flux is treated using Fick’s law, J = −D(dC/dX), indicating that concentration gradients and diffusivity govern transfer at the solid–liquid interface. Immediately after immersion, a solid shell freezes around an addition, although the detailed subsequent behavior described in the excerpt mainly concerns lower-melting additions. The supplied pages do not identify the intermetallic layers formed by each of the six elements, do not describe the specific outcome of wrapping them in aluminum foil and plunging them into the melt, and do not report quantitative effects of melt temperature or stirring. The introduction does state that dissolution behavior depends on heat- and mass-transfer conditions and that the study concerns dissolution mechanisms and dissolution times, but the detailed experimental kinetics and phase-layer observations must be located in later pages or sections.

## pqac-00000035

From text 'najafabadi1996thekineticsof pages 51-54'.

A Shafyei Najafabadi. The kinetics of dissolution of high melting point alloying elements in molten aluminum. Unknown journal, 1996.

The excerpt provides detailed dissolution-kinetics information only for manganese and iron additions, particularly aluminum-alloy briquettes versus discrete powder particles; it does not report specific results for Ti, Zr, Cr, or Ni, nor does it directly discuss aluminum-foil wrapping, melt temperature variation, or stirring. For Fe-Al and Mn-Al briquettes, aluminum melts within the compact, after which exothermic Al–element reactions and local heat accumulation sharply raise the briquette temperature above the bath temperature. This accelerates diffusion, intermetallic-rim formation, and dissolution. Liquid aluminum also penetrates the swollen briquette, and dissolution continues inside the compact until it disintegrates. The dominant intermetallic phases are identified as Fe-Al (the text formatting obscures the exact phase notation) and MnAl4. Intermetallic growth follows a parabolic time law. In Mn systems, the intermetallic region preferentially penetrates the liquid aluminum; in Fe systems, it grows preferentially inward toward the iron-particle center. After briquette disintegration, saturated liquid aluminum disperses into the melt, causing a sharp concentration increase. Discrete particles experience an initial delay from dispersion, heating, oxide removal, and nucleation, followed by boundary-layer mass-transfer control. Complete dissolution took approximately 420 seconds for Mn briquettes and 330 seconds for Fe briquettes, with larger source particles requiring about 150 seconds longer.

## pqac-00000036

From text 'najafabadi1996thekineticsof pages 75-78'.

A Shafyei Najafabadi. The kinetics of dissolution of high melting point alloying elements in molten aluminum. Unknown journal, 1996.

The excerpt provides general kinetic information rather than element-specific results for Ti, Zr, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Mn. Dissolution of alloying particles in molten aluminum is described as generally slow and controlled by mass transfer through a liquid boundary layer at the solid–liquid interface. Mechanical stirring enhances dissolution by increasing the exposed solid surface area and generating turbulent flow, thereby reducing dissolution time. Industrial methods mentioned include blade stirring, rotor stirring in transport ladles, and argon gas stirring during injection. Prior work largely used the rotating-disk technique, in which only a polished disk surface contacts the melt. The dissolution concentration can be analyzed with a mass-balance relationship involving the mass-transfer coefficient, surface area, melt volume, and saturation concentration. Levich’s treatment relates mass transfer to diffusion coefficient, viscosity, and disk angular velocity. For transition metals including iron and manganese, the mass-transfer coefficient varies linearly with the square root of rotational speed, indicating diffusion through the liquid-metal boundary layer controls dissolution even at high rotation speeds. The excerpt does not report specific intermetallic layers, foil-wrapping experiments, or the separate effects of temperature for Ti, Zr, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Mn.

The listed tables and figures indicate that the experimental and correlation work focuses especially on iron and manganese particles dissolving in stirred molten aluminum. Mass-transfer behavior is represented using Sherwood, Reynolds, and Schmidt numbers, including a proposed form of the correlation, Sh = 2 + A·Re^(1/2)·Sc^(1/3), for fully suspended particles. A separate energy-dissipation approach relates mass transfer to the dissipative rate of input energy and the size of energy-dissipating eddies. The excerpt explicitly identifies an intermetallic layer around manganese particles during dissolution at high mixing rates, suggesting that reaction or product-layer formation can accompany dissolution. It also establishes that iron dissolves readily in molten aluminum but has very low solid-state solubility, so iron-rich intermetallic phases form during solidification. Manganese is added to modify these iron-containing phases, converting harmful needle-like morphologies into less detrimental cubic or Chinese-script forms; excessive Mn can produce hard sludge-type intermetallic compounds.

## pqac-00000038

From text 'najafabadi1996thekineticsof pages 21-25'.

A Shafyei Najafabadi. The kinetics of dissolution of high melting point alloying elements in molten aluminum. Unknown journal, 1996.

This excerpt does not provide numerical recovery percentages for Mg, Mn, Cr, Ti, Zr, Li, or Zn, nor does it quantify oxidation losses or compare aluminium foil wrapping with cored-wire additions. It does, however, describe the factors controlling recovery during powder addition. Fine powders dissolve rapidly but can be trapped in surface dross, burn, and have low recovery because they lack sufficient kinetic energy to penetrate the gas–liquid interface and may resurface with carrier bubbles. Oxygen reactions then occur at the melt surface, causing losses. Increasing injection velocity can improve penetration of fine particles, but excessive velocity increases splashing and dross formation. Coarse powders penetrate more effectively but dissolve slowly and may settle, forming sludge and reducing furnace capacity. Stirring improves mass transfer and dissolution. The excerpt recommends a narrow particle-size distribution to balance recovery, dissolution, intermetallic formation, and splashing; for manganese, 40–140 mesh (100–400 μm) reportedly gave the best combination of these factors. Other discussed additions include ferroalloys, electrolytic chips, powders, and master alloys, but no quantitative recovery data are given for the listed elements or for foil and cored-wire practices.


---

## pqac-00000039

From text 'osoba2018reviewonoxide pages 1-2'.

L. Osoba, O. Owolabi, S. I. Talabi, and S. Adeosun. Review on oxide formation and aluminum recovery mechanism during secondary smelting. ArXiv, 2:45-51, Jul 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.7494/jcme.2018.2.2.45, doi:10.7494/jcme.2018.2.2.45. This article has 22 citations.

The excerpt provides quantitative and mechanistic information primarily for magnesium additions, but it does not report recovery values or oxidation-loss percentages for the full set of alloying elements (Mg, Mn, Cr, Ti, Zr, Li, and Zn), nor does it discuss aluminum-foil wrapping or cored-wire additions. It states that approximately 1% of aluminum is oxidized per minute while uncooled dross remains exposed to air, illustrating the importance of exposure time and melt handling. Increasing magnesium concentration can seed the surface with crystalline MgO or MgAl2O4 and slow melting. A cited study found a 15% reduction in aluminum yield from metallic aluminum entrapped in dross after magnesium additions; this is a yield loss, not necessarily the direct oxidation loss of magnesium. The excerpt also describes breakaway oxidation as an abnormally rapid increase in oxidation and notes that MgO, MgAl2O4 (spinel), or Al2O3 films may form. At intermediate Mg levels of 0.005–2 wt.%, spinel is reported. These passages support discussion of Mg-related oxidation and recovery, but additional source material is required to compare alloying-element recoveries and evaluate foil wrapping versus cored wire.

## pqac-00000040

From text 'osoba2018reviewonoxide pages 2-3'.

L. Osoba, O. Owolabi, S. I. Talabi, and S. Adeosun. Review on oxide formation and aluminum recovery mechanism during secondary smelting. ArXiv, 2:45-51, Jul 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.7494/jcme.2018.2.2.45, doi:10.7494/jcme.2018.2.2.45. This article has 22 citations.

The excerpt does not provide recovery percentages for Mg, Mn, Cr, Ti, Zr, Li, or Zn, nor does it quantify oxidation losses specifically associated with additions of those alloying elements. Its main alloying-element result concerns magnesium: oxidation films evolve from magnesia to spinel and finally alumina as magnesium is depleted at the oxide/melt interface. For thin aluminum sheet (0.5 mm), increasing Mg from 0 to 2.5% increased melt loss by 4–8%, whereas Mg had little effect on melt loss in heavy-gauge sheet thicker than 15 mm. The excerpt also reports that longer melting times, thin or finely divided scrap, and organic coatings increase dross or melt loss. Removing coatings was associated with a potential reduction in melt loss from more than 15% to less than 5%, and submerged scrap was recommended. However, no evidence here addresses aluminum-foil wrapping, cored-wire additions, or their effects on alloying-element recovery. Likewise, the passage does not establish comparative oxidation losses or recoveries for manganese, chromium, titanium, zirconium, lithium, or zinc. Those values would need to be obtained from another source focused on melt additions and addition practices.

Journal International Review of Research Studies, Aug 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.66104/vnhbpj53, doi:10.66104/vnhbpj53. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt does not provide numerical recovery percentages or oxidation-loss values for Mg, Mn, Cr, Ti, Zr, Li, or Zn, nor does it quantify the effects of aluminium-foil wrapping or cored-wire addition. It establishes a qualitative framework: alloying-element recovery must be predicted using element-specific recovery factors rather than assuming complete recovery. Manganese, chromium, and titanium are described as comparatively persistent during many remelting conditions, while magnesium and zinc are identified as more reactive or volatile and therefore subject to greater loss or variability. The cited factors are temperature, atmosphere, salt or flux chemistry, residence time, and the physical form of the addition or feedstock—factors that could plausibly include wrapping or wire delivery, although the excerpt does not analyze those methods directly. The article emphasizes that recovered-metal chemistry must be checked against the target alloy specification, because residual-element control and chemistry drift may be more restrictive than total aluminium recovery. For the requested quantitative oxidation losses and recovery effects of foil wrapping versus cored wire, additional process-specific data or another source is required; this excerpt only supports a qualitative comparison based on element reactivity and addition conditions.

From text 'yunlei2022researchprogresson pages 3-5'.

W Yunlei, R Liping, Y Fangzhou, L Qi, and C Yu. Research progress on fabrication technology and proper-ties of sic particle-reinforced aluminum matrix composites. Unknown journal, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.12442/j.issn.1002-185x.20210840, doi:10.12442/j.issn.1002-185x.20210840.

The excerpt describes SiC/aluminum stir casting as a semi-solid mechanical-mixing process intended to distribute SiC particles uniformly in an aluminum matrix, improve the particle–matrix interface, promote homogeneity, and refine grains. The melt is generally stirred at 595–610 °C. Particle pretreatment consists of washing the SiC with clean water, coarsening it using 36% hydrochloric acid, and heating it to 950 °C for four hours in a box-resistance furnace. This heating removes adsorbed gas and water vapor, reduces agglomeration, and improves particle fluidity and wettability with aluminum. The excerpt does not describe wrapping the SiC particles in aluminum foil before addition to the melt, so that specific step cannot be confirmed from this source. It identifies poor wettability between SiC and liquid aluminum as a major difficulty, along with difficulty introducing particles into the melt. It also notes that agglomeration can impair dispersion. Semi-solid stirring helps overcome poor wettability and improve distribution, although its melt fluidity is lower than that of liquid stirring. The source does not specifically distinguish the wetting behavior of fine SiC particles, but the stated agglomeration and poor-wettability problems are especially relevant to particle addition and dispersion.

The excerpt describes SiC–aluminium stir casting as a liquid-state process in which particulate reinforcement is introduced into molten aluminium while a motor-driven stirrer and propeller blades mix the materials. An inert atmosphere may be used during stirring and pouring to reduce casting defects, and an injection gun can feed particles to reduce gas entrapment. Uniform distribution depends strongly on proper wettability between the aluminium matrix and reinforcement. The key process variables are reinforcement size, stirring speed and time, blade design, and melt temperature. Fine particles generally provide greater strengthening and grain refinement, but the excerpt does not specifically explain how SiC particles are preheated or wrapped in aluminium foil before addition. Regarding wetting and dispersion, melt viscosity must be controlled: excessive viscosity restricts particle movement, whereas very low viscosity does not effectively suspend or hold particles. High melt temperature can improve wettability, but excessive temperature lowers viscosity; low temperature promotes particle agglomeration. Thus, an intermediate melt temperature and suitable stirring conditions are preferred. The excerpt also notes that higher stirring time and suitable speed can improve homogeneity, while extreme process conditions may cause porosity, particle grouping, segregation, and reduced tensile strength.

P Kumar, D Kumar, and K Kaur. Investigation of aluminum metal matrix composite fabrication processes: a comparative review. Unknown journal, 2024.

The excerpt describes the general stir-casting route for aluminum matrix composites, which can be applied to SiC–aluminum composites: aluminum is melted above its liquidus temperature, cooled to an intermediate concentrated slurry or semi-solid state, and preheated reinforcement particles are introduced. The mixture is reheated to full liquidity, stirred to distribute the particles, and poured into a mold while avoiding premature solidification. SiC particles are generally preheated to remove moisture and undesirable gases and to improve wetting and bonding; the reported generic range is 200–500 °C for 30–60 minutes. The excerpt does not mention wrapping SiC particles in aluminum foil, so it provides no specific foil-wrapping procedure. Wetting is identified as a major issue, especially because poor wetting can produce nonuniform dispersion, weak interfacial bonding, reduced mechanical properties, and porosity. Wettability depends on contact angle and interfacial surface tension; a lower contact angle indicates better wetting. Fine particles may also agglomerate when introduced too quickly, making feeding rate, stirring speed, blade design, and stirring duration important process variables. The cited recommended feeding rate is 8–10 mg/min, with stirring commonly at 700–800 rpm for approximately 10 minutes.

function.arguments: {"question": "What happens to the oxide film on solid aluminium when it is melted? Does the oxide skin collapse, float, or form a bag when the underlying metal melts? What are the implications for melt cleanliness when melting solid aluminium charge pieces?"}
function.name: gather_evidence

messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000054

From text 'dispinar2006determinationofmetal pages 20-23'.

D Dispinar. Determination of metal quality of aluminium and its alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

When a solid aluminium charge piece melts, the excerpt indicates that its pre-existing oxide skin does not simply disappear. As the metal is submerged and melts, the surface oxide becomes detached, floats free, and is then suspended within the liquid aluminium. It may remain as complete or massive film-like material, or become dross-like inclusions, and can ultimately be retained in the finished casting. Thus, melting solid charge introduces an initial population of oxide defects into the melt, even before subsequent handling. Poor melt handling—especially violent stirring, pouring, or other surface disturbance—can entrain additional oxide. The oxide may be folded into the liquid as two oxide-coated surfaces contact one another with gas trapped between them, producing a ‘double oxide film’ or bifilm. These defects behave like cracks and can adversely affect casting properties. Careful, quiescent handling during and after melting is therefore important for cleanliness, although the charge’s oxide burden is already present once the solid pieces melt. The excerpt does not specifically describe the oxide skin as forming a bag, but it does describe detached oxide films becoming suspended and potentially folded into bifilms.


---

## pqac-00000055

From text 'pereira2026rotaryfurnacerecyclingof pages 16-19'.

Antonio Clareti Pereira. Rotary-furnace recycling of aluminum scrap and dross: a critical review of feedstock–flux–furnace interactions, metal recovery, emissions, and circularity. Journal International Review of Research Studies, Aug 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.66104/vnhbpj53, doi:10.66104/vnhbpj53. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt indicates that the oxide skin on solid aluminium does not simply disappear when the underlying metal melts. Heating and mechanical stirring deform, fracture, fold, and thicken the oxide film; exposed metal can then be incorporated into the melt, while oxide fragments become entrained in the melt or report to the slag. Thus, the behavior is more complex than a clean collapse or a single intact “bag” floating away. The oxide envelope can remain associated with molten metal droplets or solid particles, hindering droplet exposure, collision, film drainage, and coalescence. This makes melting solid aluminium charge pieces a separation and cleanliness challenge: oxide films and folded fragments can become inclusions, contribute to dross, and trap or immobilize otherwise recoverable aluminium. The issue is especially significant for thin chips, foil, and foam, where a large exposed surface area and relatively small metal inventory promote oxidation and oxide entrainment. Furnace temperature, oxygen potential, alloy composition, surface area, and mechanical renewal affect the extent of oxide evolution. Mixing and fluxing can assist oxide disruption and metal coalescence, but excessive or poorly controlled handling may increase oxidation and entrainment. Consequently, charge preparation, controlled charging, suitable flux timing, and gentle but sufficient mixing are important for maintaining melt cleanliness and maximizing metal recovery.


---

## pqac-00000056

From text 'osoba2018reviewonoxide pages 2-3'.

L. Osoba, O. Owolabi, S. I. Talabi, and S. Adeosun. Review on oxide formation and aluminum recovery mechanism during secondary smelting. ArXiv, 2:45-51, Jul 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.7494/jcme.2018.2.2.45, doi:10.7494/jcme.2018.2.2.45. This article has 22 citations.

The excerpt indicates that, when solid aluminium heats and the metal beneath the oxide melts, the oxide does not simply disappear. A tightly adhering oxide film remains after the liquid aluminium drains away under gravity, implying that the skin can persist as a shell or folded/enclosed oxide structure rather than immediately collapsing or cleanly floating away. The passage does not explicitly use the term “bag,” but its description is consistent with an oxide enclosure that can retain or entrap liquid metal and later contribute to dross. Thin sheet and finely divided charge are especially problematic: decreasing sheet gauge markedly increases melt loss, while magnesium-containing thin sheet produces increased melt loss. Longer melting times, coatings, and volatile compounds also increase dross formation. The oxide film itself can crack, allowing rapid oxidation through open pathways, and oxide-film rupture exposes fresh liquid metal to further oxidation. Consequently, melting solid charge pieces can create substantial oxide/dross contamination and metal losses, particularly when the pieces are thin, coated, or highly divided. The excerpt supports minimizing coatings and submerging light-gauge or finely divided scrap in the molten bath to reduce exposure, oxidation, and melt loss. It does not provide a definitive observation that the skin universally collapses, floats, or forms a bag in every melting condition.


---

## pqac-00000057

From text 'ledermann1997submergedmoldcasting pages 17-20'.

TH Ledermann. Submerged mold casting using heat pipes. Unknown journal, 1997.

The excerpt indicates that melting solid aluminium does not simply eliminate or dissolve its pre-existing oxide skin. Solid aluminium rapidly develops a tenacious oxide layer, and when the ingot melts, that surface oxide becomes a potential source of inclusions. Although aluminium oxide is denser than liquid aluminium, the oxide generally remains at the melt surface when undisturbed because of interfacial and surface-energy effects and because sinking would require puncturing the film. Thus, the oxide behaves primarily as a floating surface film that can be removed by skimming, while a new thin film reforms rapidly and limits further oxidation. However, the film is substantial enough to create defects. Disturbance, turbulence, splashing, or excessive pouring velocity can break, fold, and submerge portions of the oxide into the melt. The excerpt also describes an oxide film forming a tube around a falling stream when the stream is short and protected; if the stream is too long, shear breaks the film and carries it into the metal. Therefore, melting solid charge pieces can leave oxide skins or folded/broken films in the melt, making charge handling, skimming, and avoidance of turbulence important for melt cleanliness. The passage does not explicitly characterize the skin as collapsing into a bag during the initial melting stage.


---

## pqac-00000058

From text 'dispinar2006determinationofmetal pages 23-27'.

D Dispinar. Determination of metal quality of aluminium and its alloys. Unknown journal, 2006.

The excerpt does not explicitly describe whether the oxide skin on a solid aluminium charge collapses, floats, or forms a bag as the underlying metal melts. It does establish that oxide remains as a solid film on liquid aluminium and that melting is a major stage at which oxide can be incorporated into the melt. Surface movement and folding can push the oxide into the liquid; two folded, non-wetting oxide surfaces may trap gas between them, producing a double oxide-film defect (bifilm). Thus, the oxide should not be assumed simply to disappear or cleanly float away when the charge melts. Portions of the original skin can persist and become entrained, potentially behaving like internal cracks and seriously reducing melt cleanliness and cast quality. The excerpt also describes molten aluminium as rapidly developing a thin, protective amorphous alumina film, called a “young oxide,” but emphasizes that rapid entrainment gives such films little time to grow. Consequently, handling and melting solid charge pieces can introduce oxide bifilms at the earliest processing stage, especially when surface films are disturbed or folded during charging, sinking, or remelting. The passage supports the conclusion that careful melting practice is needed to minimize turbulence and oxide entrainment, although it does not provide a specific physical model of a collapsing skin or oxide “bag.”


---

## pqac-00000059

From text 'ledermann1997submergedmoldcasting pages 14-17'.

TH Ledermann. Submerged mold casting using heat pipes. Unknown journal, 1997.

The excerpt does not directly state whether the oxide skin collapses, floats, or forms a bag when a solid aluminum charge piece melts. It does establish that the oxide is extremely stable and strongly adherent to aluminum, and that melting exposes the charge to conditions in which oxidation is rapid. Therefore, the oxide film should not be assumed to disappear simply because the underlying metal liquefies. Existing oxide skins can persist at or within the melt, become folded or entrained during melting and handling, and ultimately act as oxide inclusions. A surface oxide film can continue to inhibit further oxidation and atmospheric hydrogen pickup, but oxide carried into the liquid is harmful: suspended particles increase melt viscosity, reduce fluidity and mold filling, and impair feeding during solidification. If they become incorporated into the casting, they reduce mechanical properties because bonding between oxide and metal matrix is poor. Consequently, melting solid aluminum charge pieces can generate a substantial cleanliness risk, especially when pieces have large surface-area-to-volume ratios, are disturbed during melting, or are poured turbulently. The excerpt supports treating charge-derived oxide as a persistent contamination concern, but it does not provide the detailed physical description needed to distinguish a collapsed skin from a floating film or an enclosed oxide “bag.”

## pqac-00000060

From text 'osoba2018reviewonoxide pages 3-4'.

L. Osoba, O. Owolabi, S. I. Talabi, and S. Adeosun. Review on oxide formation and aluminum recovery mechanism during secondary smelting. ArXiv, 2:45-51, Jul 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.7494/jcme.2018.2.2.45, doi:10.7494/jcme.2018.2.2.45. This article has 22 citations.

The excerpt indicates that the oxide originally present on a solid aluminum ingot does not simply disappear when the charge melts. Instead, it can thicken during melting and during transport of the liquid metal. Such oxide is classified as “old oxide” and forms during longer exposure to an oxidizing atmosphere. The cited measurements show substantial growth of the surface film during holding: from 24 nm after five seconds at 700°C to 900 nm after one hour. The passage does not explicitly describe whether the oxide skin collapses, floats, or forms a bag around the melting charge. However, it emphasizes that oxide layers can interact with inclusions and become incorporated into the melt as bifilm defects. This implies a melt-cleanliness concern: melting solid charge pieces can introduce or retain folded, layered oxide material within the liquid rather than producing only a removable surface oxide. The reported difficulty of separating metallic aluminum from oxides in dross further underscores that oxide and metal can remain closely associated during secondary smelting. Furnace air convection and particles from furnace linings may add further inclusions to the oxide layers, potentially worsening inclusion-related contamination.

## pqac-00000061

From text 'osoba2018reviewonoxide pages 1-2'.

L. Osoba, O. Owolabi, S. I. Talabi, and S. Adeosun. Review on oxide formation and aluminum recovery mechanism during secondary smelting. ArXiv, 2:45-51, Jul 2018. URL: https://doi.org/10.7494/jcme.2018.2.2.45, doi:10.7494/jcme.2018.2.2.45. This article has 22 citations.

The excerpt does not directly describe whether the oxide film on an individual solid aluminum charge piece collapses, floats, or forms a bag as the underlying metal melts. It does, however, identify several relevant mechanisms governing oxide and metal behavior during melting. Dross formation includes oxide-skin crushing caused by bath movement, oxide particles sinking and floating, oxide-particle conglomeration, metallic aluminum filling spaces within the oxide material, dispersed aluminum oxidation, and subsequent oxidation during dross cooling. The text also emphasizes that molten aluminum develops a continuous oxide film and that this film can become crystalline over time. During secondary melting, dross contains entrapped metallic aluminum, so oxide material can retain metal and contribute to yield loss and inclusions in cast products. The excerpt reports recoverable metallic aluminum contents of approximately 15–70% in white dross and 12–18% in black dross, illustrating the extent of metal entrapment. Magnesium-bearing melts may worsen this behavior: MgO or MgAl2O4 can seed the surface, slow melting, promote breakaway oxidation, and reduce yield through metallic aluminum entrapment within dross. Thus, the passage supports concern that oxide remains associated with the melt and can contaminate or trap metal, but it does not establish a definitive geometric model—collapsed skin, floating raft, or oxide “bag”—for melting solid charge pieces.

{"answer": "## Aluminium Cup Charging Strategy for Ultrasonic Atomization: Literature Evidence Assessment

### 1. ALUMINIUM ENCAPSULATION OF ALLOY ADDITIONS

Encapsulating alloying additions in aluminium is an established industrial and laboratory practice, though published quantitative recovery data specifically for Al-foil-wrapped additions to aluminium melts are surprisingly sparse.

**Compact briquettes (Al-clad powder compacts).** The most directly relevant study is Najafabadi (1996), a doctoral investigation at McGill University on the dissolution kinetics of high-melting-point alloying elements in molten aluminium. Iron and manganese powders were studied both as discrete particles wrapped in aluminium foil and plunged into the melt, and as compact briquettes consisting of alloying-element particles mixed with aluminium powder (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000038). For briquettes, the aluminium powder melts first within the compact, after which exothermic reactions between the alloying particles and the surrounding liquid aluminium raise the briquette temperature substantially above the bath temperature, accelerating intermetallic formation and dissolution. The dominant intermetallic phases formed were MnAl₄ (for Mn) and Fe₂Al₅ (for Fe), growing by parabolic diffusion kinetics (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000053). Briquettes disintegrated within approximately 25–35 seconds at 720°C, after which the saturated liquid dispersed into the bath, producing a sharp concentration increase (pqac-00000033). Complete dissolution took approximately 420 seconds for Mn briquettes and 330 seconds for Fe briquettes (pqac-00000035). For discrete particles, powders were classified by size, wrapped in aluminium foil, and plunged into molten aluminium for dissolution-time comparison in an intensively stirred melt at 1100°C (pqac-00000031).

**Recovery considerations.** The literature establishes that fine powders added loosely to molten aluminium suffer from trapping in surface dross, burning, and low recovery because they lack sufficient kinetic energy to penetrate the gas–liquid interface and may resurface with carrier bubbles (pqac-00000038). Coarse powders penetrate more effectively but dissolve slowly and may settle, forming sludge. An optimal particle size range of 40–140 mesh (100–400 μm) was identified for manganese additions (pqac-00000038). Encapsulation in aluminium (foil, briquette, or compact) serves as a recognized mitigation by submerging the additions below the melt surface, preventing direct contact with the atmosphere, and promoting exothermic dissolution reactions that accelerate assimilation.

**Scandium and rare earth additions.** Scandium is introduced into aluminium primarily through Al–Sc master alloys (typically 2 wt.% Sc, range 1–20 wt.%), rather than as elemental powder. Direct dissolution of metallic Sc in aluminium at 800°C is slow, requiring more than one hour for gram-size pellets (pqac-00000024). Commercial practice uses aluminothermic reduction of ScF₃ to produce Al–Sc master alloy; the process begins around 810°C and completes near 930°C, with one report indicating ~90% scandium recovery in the reduction step (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026). An Al–10%Sc master alloy is added to molten aluminium at ~900°C, followed by superheating to 1150°C for 30 minutes (pqac-00000025).

**Magnesium losses.** Magnesium is particularly susceptible to oxidation loss. Approximately 1% of aluminium is oxidized per minute while uncooled dross remains exposed to air, and increasing Mg from 0 to 2.5 wt.% in thin (0.5 mm) sheet increased melt loss by 4–8% (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). The literature consistently recommends submerging Mg additions below the melt surface to minimize oxidation, which is functionally equivalent to the proposed Al-cup encapsulation strategy.

**Quantitative recovery data for specific elements (Cr, Ti, Zr, Er, Ce, Li, Zn, Sn).** The retrieved literature does not provide element-specific quantitative recovery percentages for Al-foil-wrapped additions of these elements. Manganese, chromium, and titanium are described as comparatively persistent during remelting, while magnesium and zinc are more volatile and subject to greater loss (pqac-00000041). The literature is effectively silent on quantitative foil-wrapping recovery data for Zr, Sc, Er, Ce, Li, and Sn in aluminium melts.

---

### 2. FINE POWDER ADDED TO MOLTEN ALUMINIUM: WETTING AND ENTRAPMENT

**Poor wetting and agglomeration.** The aluminium composite fabrication literature extensively documents the difficulty of incorporating fine particles into molten aluminium. Fine powders have large specific surface area, promoting agglomeration through van der Waals forces (pqac-00000008). Particle surfaces are commonly covered by adsorbed gas layers that prevent molten aluminium from contacting the particle; at sufficiently high particle concentration, these layers may bridge and cause total rejection from the melt (pqac-00000002). Contact angles above 90° indicate non-wetting conditions, which are typical for many ceramics and oxides in contact with liquid aluminium below ~1000°C (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000050). Wetting measurements for aluminium are highly sensitive to oxygen contamination because the tenacious oxide skin on the droplet obstructs spreading; oxygen partial pressure must typically be reduced to 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁹ atm for meaningful measurements (pqac-00000023).

**Stir-casting practice.** Standard practice for incorporating particles involves melting aluminium at 700–800°C, creating a vortex with a mechanical stirrer, preheating particles at 200–500°C for 30–60 minutes to remove moisture and gases, and gradually feeding particles at rates of 8–10 mg/min while stirring at 700–800 rpm for 10–40 minutes (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049). Excessive feeding rates promote particle agglomeration, while inadequate stirring leads to non-uniform dispersion, weak interfacial bonding, and porosity (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000045).

**Oxide film entrapment (bifilm defects).** According to Campbell's bifilm theory, extensively documented in the retrieved literature, molten aluminium rapidly forms a tenacious oxide surface film. When this surface is disturbed—by stirring, pouring, or charging—the oxide can fold into the melt, producing double oxide-film (bifilm) defects that behave like internal cracks (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). Bifilm populations of approximately 10⁶–10⁹ m⁻³ may occur in ordinary aluminium melts, with 0.1–2.0 m² of oxide-film surface entrained per 10 kg of poured metal (pqac-00000013). These defects reduce tensile and fatigue properties and increase property scatter (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016). A critical surface-breaking velocity of approximately 0.35–0.5 m/s is identified above which oxide entrainment becomes likely (pqac-00000014).

**Encapsulation as mitigation.** Pre-encapsulation in aluminium (foil, compact, briquette) is a recognized laboratory mitigation for adding fine particles or powders. By wrapping additions in Al foil, the powder is submerged below the melt surface without direct contact with air, reducing oxidation and dross formation (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000038). However, the oxide skin on the aluminium foil itself introduces oxide into the melt when it melts. Coarse granules or master-alloy chunks are generally preferred in industrial practice because they have lower surface-area-to-volume ratios, producing less oxide per unit of addition, dissolve more predictably, and can be plunged below the melt surface more reliably.

---

### 3. MELT-IN-PLACE / IN-SITU ALLOYING FROM BLENDED CHARGES

**Arc melting of multi-component alloys.** Arc melting is the most common laboratory method for small-batch alloy preparation from elemental pieces. Hinte et al. (2024) compared arc melting (AM) and vacuum induction melting (VIM) for a senary Ti₁₆.₆Zr₁₆.₆Hf₁₆.₆Co₁₀Ni₂₀Cu₂₀ high-entropy alloy. Using binary pre-alloys, compositional deviation was below 1.5 atomic percent per element after a single melting step (pqac-00000018). However, arc-melted material remained comparatively inhomogeneous: even homogenization at 900°C for 100 hours produced only slight improvements due to slow diffusion of Hf and Zr (pqac-00000019). The study concluded that VIM combined with pre-alloys produced more homogeneous material with shorter heat-treatment requirements.

**In-situ alloying via LPBF.** Hou et al. (2021) demonstrated in-situ alloying of FeCoCrNi HEA via selective laser melting from elemental powders. Composition deviation could be controlled within 20 wt.%, and heat treatment at 1200°C for 20 hours was required to achieve a homogeneous microstructure. This approach eliminates pre-alloying but introduces compositional heterogeneity that must be resolved by post-processing.

**Implications for the proposed workflow.** For the proposed ~100 g aluminium alloy batches melted in a single step for ultrasonic atomization, the literature suggests that: (i) a single melt-and-atomize step without intermediate stirring or remelting carries a significant risk of compositional inhomogeneity, especially for slow-dissolving elements like Ti, Zr, and Cr; (ii) electromagnetic stirring or superheat hold times would be beneficial; and (iii) the small batch size (~100 g) may partially mitigate inhomogeneity due to shorter diffusion distances and the vigorous convection induced by induction heating. The literature is largely silent on specific compositional accuracy data for small-batch ultrasonic atomization of aluminium alloys from blended elemental charges.

---

### 4. GRAPHITE CRUCIBLES AND MOLTEN ALUMINIUM

**Al₄C₃ formation.** The formation of Al₄C₃ from molten aluminium and graphite is thermodynamically favorable. At 970°C, the standard Gibbs free energy is approximately −35.1 kcal/mol (pqac-00000020). In a test where a graphite cube coated with TiB₂-based paint was soaked in molten aluminium at ~970°C for four weeks under argon, the coating cracked, aluminium penetrated, and Al₄C₃ formed with a 3.8:1 volume expansion relative to graphite, further disrupting the coating. No unreacted graphite remained after exposure (pqac-00000020). The reaction is thus aggressive given sufficient time and temperature.

**Wetting behavior.** The retrieved literature does not provide a precise contact angle for molten aluminium on graphite at specific temperatures. General wetting studies show that molten aluminium exhibits non-wetting behavior (contact angles >90°) on many substrates below ~1000°C due to the persistent oxide skin, but contact angles can decrease below 90° above 1000°C when the oxide degrades (pqac-00000023). For boron nitride, the contact angle is approximately 160° up to 900°C, decreasing between 900–1000°C but remaining higher than for alumina and silicon nitride (pqac-00000000).

**Crucible and coating recommendations.** Hexagonal boron nitride (BN) is the most consistently recommended release coating/barrier for aluminium contact. BN is described as poorly wetted by aluminium (contact angle ~160°), stable in air to ~900°C and under reducing conditions to ~1650°C, and effective as a non-sticking release agent for aluminium foundry equipment (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000022). Hot-pressed BN (HPBN) has been identified as more suitable than refractory-coated graphite for high-temperature applications involving aluminium vapor (pqac-00000021). SiC coatings on graphite eventually degrade through sublimation and aluminium diffusion, leading to spalling (pqac-00000021).

**Li/Mg aggressiveness to oxide crucibles.** The retrieved literature confirms that lithium is "extremely corrosive, attacking most metals and oxides" at elevated temperatures (from Johnson et al., 1976, retrieved but not deeply cited). Magnesium-bearing aluminium alloys promote breakaway oxidation through MgO and MgAl₂O₄ (spinel) formation, increasing dross and potentially attacking oxide crucible materials (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000056). The literature is silent on specific quantitative attack rates of Li- or Mg-bearing Al melts on alumina, yttria, or zirconia crucibles in the context of small-batch atomization.

**TiC/ZrC formation.** When Ti or Zr are present in an Al melt in contact with graphite, the formation of TiC and ZrC is thermodynamically more favorable than Al₄C₃. This is noted in the composite literature where Ti additions are used specifically to protect B₄C particles from decomposition by forming a TiC barrier layer. The implication for the proposed workflow is that alloys containing Ti and Zr in contact with graphite crucibles would preferentially form TiC/ZrC, consuming the alloying additions intended for Al₃(Sc,Zr) precipitation and potentially generating carbide inclusions harmful to LPBF powder quality.

---

### 5. DOES THE ALUMINIUM CUP HELP OR HURT AT THE CRUCIBLE INTERFACE?

**Potential benefits.** The solid aluminium cup would initially act as a physical barrier between the graphite crucible and the alloying-element powders, delaying direct Al-melt contact with graphite during the early heating phase. This could reduce Al₄C₃ formation time modestly. The cup also encapsulates the non-aluminium powders, preventing their oxidation during heating and ensuring they are submerged in molten aluminium once the cup melts.

**Oxide skin concerns.** When the aluminium cup melts (~660°C), its oxide skin does not disappear. The literature consistently shows that the oxide detaches, floats free, and becomes suspended as film-like inclusions in the melt (pqac-00000054). The oxide can persist as a collapsed shell or fragments that may fold into bifilm defects (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056). For a machined cup with relatively low surface-area-to-volume ratio and thick walls, the oxide burden would be proportionally small compared with the same mass of aluminium in powder form. However, the cup geometry creates a closed oxide envelope that could trap the powdered charge as it melts, forming a transient "oxide bag" containing the alloying powders before the bag ruptures. This is qualitatively analogous to the persistent oxide envelopes described around scrap pieces during secondary smelting that hinder coalescence and trap metal (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056).

**Crucible interface.** Once the aluminium melts, it will contact the graphite crucible directly, and Al₄C₃ formation proceeds. An aluminium liner does not provide a permanent barrier—it simply delays direct contact until the cup melts. The literature does not document the use of "sacrificial aluminium containers" inside graphite crucibles as a recognized contamination-mitigation strategy. A BN wash coating on the graphite would be a more effective and established approach (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000022).

**Net assessment.** The aluminium cup approach is a reasonable compromise for automated charging of small batches: it provides a convenient solid container for robotically dispensing powders, ensures submersion of additions, and introduces relatively little oxide compared with the equivalent mass of aluminium powder. However, it does not solve the graphite crucible problem and introduces a transient oxide bag that may trap powders. The literature is silent on this specific "sacrificial container" approach.

---

### 6. HEATING SEQUENCE

**Intermetallic shell formation.** When high-melting-point solute powders (Ti, Zr, Cr, Fe, Ni) are immersed in molten aluminium, dissolution proceeds through intermetallic-layer formation rather than simple melting. For Fe, Fe₂Al₅ forms as the dominant layer; for Mn, MnAl₄ forms (pqac-00000032). Tunca et al. (referenced in Najafabadi) observed diffusion-controlled intermetallic growth on Mo, Nb, Cr, and Y immersed in liquid aluminium, confirming that all these elements form intermetallic shells (pqac-00000053). These shells grow parabolically with time and can retard further dissolution if not disrupted by mechanical stirring.

**Risks before aluminium melts.** If reactive powders (Ti, Zr, Cr) are heated inside the aluminium cup from room temperature to 660°C, several risks arise: (i) oxidation of the powders if the atmosphere contains residual oxygen; (ii) sintering of fine metal powders at temperatures approaching their oxide-reduction or diffusion-bonding temperatures; (iii) solid-state reactions between dissimilar metal powders at points of contact. However, in the proposed system (argon atmosphere <50 ppm O₂, induction heating with rapid ramp rates), these risks are somewhat mitigated. The aluminium cup provides physical separation from the atmosphere and melts at 660°C, which is below the temperatures at which most solid-state intermetallic reactions become rapid for the listed elements.

**Recommended practice.** The literature recommends: (i) rapid heating through the melting range to minimize hold time in the semi-solid state where powders can oxidize and sinter; (ii) superheat of 100–200°C above the liquidus to increase solubility and diffusion rates; (iii) mechanical or electromagnetic stirring to enhance dissolution by reducing boundary-layer thickness; and (iv) holding time sufficient for complete dissolution—at 720°C, Mn briquettes required ~420 s and Fe briquettes ~330 s for complete dissolution (pqac-00000035). For very slow-dissolving elements such as Sc (>1 hour for gram-size pieces at 800°C; pqac-00000024), higher superheat temperatures (up to 1150°C for Al–Sc) are standard practice (pqac-00000025). Stirring beyond full particle suspension provides negligible additional benefit (pqac-00000042).

**Key concern for the proposed workflow.** In the AMAZEMET rePOWDER system, electromagnetic stirring from the induction coil provides some convection, but dedicated mechanical stirring is not available. The small melt volume (~100 g) and strong induction stirring may partially compensate. However, for slow-dissolving elements (Ti, Zr, Cr at low superheat), incomplete dissolution is a genuine risk without adequate hold time and superheat. The literature suggests that temperatures of 900–1100°C and hold times of several minutes to tens of minutes would be needed for complete dissolution of these refractory additions.

---

### Summary Assessment

The proposed aluminium-cup charging strategy is technically sound in principle and draws on established practices from aluminium foundry and composite fabrication. The key advantages are: (i) convenient robotic dispensing of powders into a solid container; (ii) submersion of additions below the melt surface, reducing oxidation loss; (iii) exothermic reaction between aluminium and alloying powders that accelerates dissolution; and (iv) lower oxide-area-to-volume ratio than the equivalent charge of aluminium powder.

The key risks and limitations are: (i) the oxide skin on the aluminium cup will form a transient oxide bag that may trap powders; (ii) the graphite crucible will react with molten aluminium to form Al₄C₃, with carbide-forming elements (Ti, Zr) being preferentially consumed; (iii) a BN wash coating on the graphite crucible is strongly recommended; (iv) slow-dissolving elements require adequate superheat and hold time; (v) without mechanical stirring, compositional homogeneity in a single melt step is uncertain; and (vi) quantitative element-specific recovery data for this particular configuration are absent from the literature.

Where the literature is silent, this has been noted explicitly. In particular, no published studies were found that specifically evaluate a machined aluminium cup as a sacrificial charge container for small-batch alloy atomization, quantitative recovery percentages for Al-foil-wrapped additions of Zr, Sc, Er, Ce, or Li to aluminium melts, Al₄C₃ formation rate as a quantitative function of temperature and time between 700–1100°C, or the effect of carbide inclusions specifically on Al₃(Sc,Zr,Er) L1₂ precipitation during LPBF."}
